hook_text: The picture on the back of your eye is upside down. You have never noticed, because your brain is doing the real seeing.
clip_script: Light enters your eye through the cornea, a clear curved window that does most of the focusing. The iris, the coloured ring, squeezes the pupil small in sunshine and opens it wide in the dark. The lens fine-tunes the focus, fat for your phone, thin for the board. The light lands on the retina, and here is the surprise: the picture is upside down, exactly like a pinhole camera. The retina is lined with millions of tiny receptor cells. Rods work in dim light but see only grey, which is why a dark cinema looks colourless. Cones need more light but see colour and detail. When light hits them, they fire nerve impulses down the optic nerve to the back of your brain, and only there does the picture appear, the right way up. You do not see with your eyes. You see with your brain.
visual_style: A whiteboard eye cross-section with a ray of light passing cornea, pupil and lens to an inverted image on the retina, then a zoom into rods and cones firing signals along the optic nerve to a brain.
pacing: A steady journey through the eye, ending on a punchy reveal.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find your own blind spot.
